Well, today I’ll explain where this miracle drug that’s saving lives comes from and why it’s effective.

As the media is being forced to admit, it’s been around for, like, forever, but it was used to treat parasites. For those of you who remember high school biology, parasites are classified as animals due to the nature of their cell membranes. Animals are unique among the kingdoms in that they have a double phospholipid layer as their only barrier between their ‘insides’ and their ‘outsides’. The cells interact with their environments using special carrier proteins.

One of the reasons hospitals inject saline (0.9% salt water) rather than straight water is because the cell membrane is filled with pores that allow water to pass freely by osmosis. If you give a solution that is too salty, the cells shrink and the water balance inside is disrupted. If you give a solution that is too pure, the cells expand and burst.

Why is this important? Because of the way viruses interact with the cell.

There was some debate as to whether viruses are alive or dead. In my opinion, if they evolve (and the flu proves that they do), then they must be considered alive. They are obligate parasites which interact with their hosts by attaching a protein carrier to the exterior of the cell membrane. They then inject their contents (usually DNA or RNA) into the cell, where the mechanisms of the cell take over and make more viruses until the cell bursts.

Now, there was some hysteria about the fact that Covid can reinfect people who have recovered. This is a nothing burger. Viruses do that all the time, especially viruses of the herpes family (not just genital herpes, but also things like measles, mumps, chickenpox and shingles). It’s the main mechanism by which viruses remain in their host populations.

Coronaviruses are not new to science. They are in fact so common that until the outbreak of Covid they weren’t routinely tested for (which is one of the reasons there are no “Kits,” as I explained yesterday).

What makes Covid dangerous is the novelty of the proteins in the protein carrier. Most people with healthy immune systems will adapt without issue, which is why the recovery rate is so high among those populations. It also accounts for the delay between the onset of the infectious period and the symptomatic phase, and why many people exhibit no symptoms at all.

The exception of course is the immunocompromised and the elderly (who are also, by definition, immunocompromised).

Now, going back to these miracle drugs. Remember when I said that the infections they are approved to treat are caused by animals, compared to bacteria, viruses or fungi? Well, in order to be a parasite an organism has to trick the immune system of the host organism into thinking it’s harmless. This is somewhat difficult for bacteria, fungi, and viruses to do, since they’re so far removed from us by evolution.

Animals, on the other hand, are all of the same kingdom and have the same basic cell mechanisms. Their cell membranes (Not WALLS) look a lot like OUR cell membranes, and at first the immune system can’t tell the difference. It’s the same problem that makes cancer so hard to treat (because cancer is you, not an infection. Your body still has a way to deal with this, but it’s slower and takes longer to work.

The target for both bacterial infections and fungal infections is the cell wall. Which is something animals do not have, and thus makes a really good target. You can give fairly large amounts of many antibiotics or antifungals without triggering an allergic response.

At the same time, you don’t want to kill off all of the bacteria and fungus, just the stuff that’s growing where it shouldn’t be. Why? Because 90% plus of infections are caused by “normal flora” which is just growing somewhere that it shouldn’t be. Your body actually needs that shit to function properly. So the goal is just to slow the bacteria or fungus down a bit to give your immune system time to catch up.

With viruses, it’s flip-flop.

Once they’ve injected their contents into your cells’ interior, viruses are actually pretty harmless. The problem is that they trigger an immune response. That response is what causes symptoms. But viruses don’t actually want to kill you. The opposite, in fact. They want you to live long enough to spread the virus to other potential hosts. And then they want you to live long enough for your immune system to forget about them, so that they can try to reactivate and try again to infect more hosts. At any given moment (at least during cold/flu season), it’s a coin flip as to whether or not your shedding a somewhat harmless virus.

In other words, they have two basic modes. Lone wolf, and sleeper agent. Corona viruses are sleeper agents.

Think of them like spam in your inbox, or junk mail delivered to your door. If the immune system is set too tight, it blocks important messages. If it’s too broad, then it lets everything through. So in many cases, it’s necessary to let some idiot scan the first few paragraphs from the Nigerian prince until he learns better. Other times (like ebola), it’s best to burn the letter unopened.

The miracle drugs in question are used to treat a specific infection, malaria, which is somewhat unique for parasites in that it is an intracellular parasite (compared to worms or insects, as well as most bacteria). Viruses are ALSO intracellular parasites. But because viruses and animal parasites are completely different kingdoms, they trigger different immune responses.

Now, remember, Corona viruses don’t want to kill you, just infect you. Their danger comes from the novel proteins on their protein carriers, which trigger an immune response. Once you’re infected, it’s another big nothing burger. Your immune system sees it and says “Yeah, so what? I’ve dealt with your ilk before, you don’t scare me.” But if your immune system doesn’t recognize it, it comes out swinging, no holds barred. It nukes when it should snipe. It burns bridges that it needs to cross yet. It swears when it should be polite.

THAT is why this treatment works. It’s not preventing infection. It’s not killing the virus. It’s slowing down the immune system’s response and giving it an opportunity to catch up with the disease. At the same time, however, it’s important that the immune system continues business as usual in every other regards to prevent other infections from killing you.
